title: Chapter 57 — Of Whales in Paint; in Teeth; in Wood; in Sheet-Iron; in
paragraphs: On Tower Hill, as you head down to the London docks, you may have seen a crippled beggar (a kedger, as sailors call him) holding a painted board in front of him that shows the tragic scene in which he lost his leg. There are three whales and three boats, and one of the boats (supposed to hold the missing leg in all its original soundness) is being crunched in the jaws of the foremost whale. For the last ten years, they tell me, that man has held up that picture and shown off that stump to a disbelieving world. But now the time has come for him to be vindicated. His three whales are as good as any whales ever published in Wapping, at any rate, and his stump is as unquestionable a stump as any you'll find in the western clearings. Yet though he is forever mounted on that stump, the poor whaleman never makes a stump-speech; he just stands with downcast eyes, ruefully contemplating his own amputation.

Throughout the Pacific, and also in Nantucket, and New Bedford, and Sag Harbor, you will come across lively sketches of whales and whaling scenes, engraved by the fishermen themselves on Sperm Whale teeth, or on ladies' busks (corset stays) worked out of Right Whale bone, and other such skrimshander (scrimshaw) articles, as the whalemen call the numerous ingenious little objects they elaborately carve out of the rough material in their hours of ocean leisure. Some of them have little boxes of dentist-like tools, specially intended for the skrimshandering business. But in general they toil with their jackknives alone; and with that almost all-powerful tool of the sailor, they will turn out for you anything you please in the way of a mariner's fancy.

Long exile from Christendom and civilization inevitably returns a man to the condition God put him in — namely, what people call savagery. Your true whale-hunter is as much a savage as an Iroquois. I am a savage myself, loyal to no one but the King of the Cannibals, and ready to rebel against him at any moment.

Now, one of the peculiar characteristics of the savage in his domestic hours is his wonderful patience and industry. An ancient Hawaiian war-club or spear-paddle, in its full complexity and elaboration of carving, is as great a testament to human perseverance as a Latin dictionary. For with nothing but a bit of broken sea-shell or a shark's tooth, that miraculous intricacy of wooden net-work has been achieved. And it has cost steady years of steady work.

As with the Hawaiian savage, so with the white sailor-savage. With the same marvelous patience, and with the same single shark's tooth of his one poor jackknife, he will carve you a bit of bone sculpture — not quite as expertly made, but as densely packed in its maze-like design as the Greek savage Achilles's shield, and full of barbaric spirit and suggestion, as the prints of that fine old Dutch savage, Albert Durer.
Wooden whales — or whales cut in profile from small dark slabs of the noble South Sea war-wood — turn up often in the forecastles of American whalers. Some of them are made with great accuracy.

At some old gable-roofed country houses you will see brass whales hung by the tail as knockers on the roadside door. When the porter is sleepy, the anvil-headed whale would work best. But these knocking whales are seldom noteworthy as faithful likenesses. On the steeples of some old-fashioned churches you will see sheet-iron whales placed there as weather-vanes. But they are so high up, and besides are to all intents and purposes labeled "Hands off!" — so you cannot examine them closely enough to judge their merit.

In bony, ribbed regions of the earth, where masses of rock lie scattered in fantastic groups across the plain at the foot of high, broken cliffs, you will often find shapes that look like the petrified forms of Leviathan, half sunk in grass that breaks against them in a surf of green waves on a windy day.

Then again, in mountainous countries where the traveler is continually ringed by amphitheater-like heights, here and there from some lucky vantage point you will catch passing glimpses of the profiles of whales outlined along the undulating ridges. But you must be a thorough whaleman to see these sights; and not only that, but if you wish to return to such a sight again, you must be sure to take the exact intersecting latitude and longitude of your first standpoint; otherwise, so much a matter of chance are such observations of the hills, your precise earlier standpoint would require laborious rediscovery — like the Soloma Islands, which still remain unknown, though high-ruffed Mendanna once walked them and old Figuera chronicled them.

And when your subject lifts and expands your mind, you cannot help tracing great whales in the starry heavens, with boats chasing them — just as the Eastern nations, their minds long full of war, saw armies locked in battle among the clouds. So in the North I have chased Leviathan round and round the Pole, following the wheeling of the bright points that first outlined him for me. And under the blazing Antarctic skies I have boarded the Argo-Navis and joined the hunt for the starry Cetus far past the farthest reach of Hydrus and the Flying Fish.

With a frigate's anchors for my bridle-bits and bundles of harpoons for spurs, how I wish I could mount that whale and leap past the highest skies, to find out whether the fabled heavens, with all their countless tents, really lie camped beyond the reach of my mortal sight!
